author: Our World in Data
body:
The United States Geological Survey (USGS) publishes its yearly Mineral Commodity Summaries, with production and reserves data for a wide range of minerals. We combine it with the World Mineral Statistics of the British Geological Survey (BGS). Together, they cover many of the minerals that batteries, solar panels, and electric cars need, with data up to 2025.

The combined data covers more than 150 countries, with world totals for some minerals going back to 1900 and country data for many from the 1970s. We recently updated hundreds of our charts with the latest release.

This chart tracks lithium mining each year. Global lithium mining reached an estimated 290,000 tonnes in 2025, about 30% more than in 2024 and around 20 times its 2000 level. In 2025, Australia was the biggest producer with an estimated 92,000 tonnes; China and Chile came next.

(This data update was led by Pablo Rosado.)

Explore all of the updated data in our interactive charts: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/minerals

author: Our World in Data
body:
Global electricity generation has tripled since 1985 — most of this growth came from Asia.

In 1985, the world generated around 10,000 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity. In 2024, it produced just over 30,000 TWh — three times as much.

Three-quarters of this increase came from Asia. The chart shows how generation has grown, both globally and in each region.

Yes, population growth explains some of this. But two other drivers were even stronger: more people gained access to electricity, and they consumed more of it. In the early 1990s, fewer than half of South Asians had access to basic electricity. Today, access is almost universal.

At the same time, electricity generation per person increased by almost 450% — far faster than in any other region. Outside of Asia, it has barely changed. This is why, globally, per-person consumption has only doubled.

This growth has given households more and better energy services, and it has also powered a huge expansion of industry.

(written by Hannah Ritchie)

Explore how electricity generation and sources have changed across the world: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/electricity-mix

author: Aziz Sunderji
body:
Much has been written about the K-shaped economy: wealthier households pulling away from everyone else. Less noticed is how sharply this shows up in home prices within cities, along lines of income, race, schools and crime. My new map story, Pulling Apart, follows it through five cities.

In Philadelphia, prices are rising in the rich suburbs. Haddonfield, where the median household earns $151,000, is up 6.8% over the past year. By contrast, they are falling in poorer places: just across the river, in Camden, where it earns only $37,000, they are down 7.8%.

In Detroit, the split follows race. Prices are rising in mostly white suburbs: Commerce Township, under 3% Black, is up 2.7%. By contrast, they are falling in mostly Black neighborhoods: an east-side ZIP code that is 90% Black is down 12%.

In Phoenix, the divide is education. Where most adults have a bachelor's degree, prices are rising: in Paradise Valley, where 72% do, they are up 12%. Where few do, prices are falling: in West Phoenix, where only 8% do, they are down 3.2%.

In Atlanta, I ranked neighborhoods with my "fanciness" index. Prices are rising in the fanciest places: Buckhead, in the 96th percentile nationally, is up 7.6%. They are falling in the least fancy: Forest Park, in just the 6th percentile, is down 5.8%.

In Indianapolis, prices are rising in suburbs with good schools and little crime: in Carmel, students test 3.2 grade levels above average, and values are up 5.1%. They are falling in the city: the near east side tests 2.3 grade levels below, has 80 times the violent crime, and is down 4%.

I made every map here with ProMap, which you can use to explore any neighborhood in the country. The full story takes about five minutes: https://thepromap.com/story/r3c5q7
